title: The dark age is a knife
word: The dark age is a knife
hook: this age is a knife, kings are butchers, and righteousness has flown (Majh ki Var, ang 145)
tomorrow: Hard to be called a Muslim

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ballad in Majh, and your line was the majh ballad. Did you hear a song climbing its steps? Today the ballad gets to one of its hardest lines. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

The age is a knife. The kings are butchers. Righteousness has grown wings and flown away. That's one salok in Guru Nanak's ballad in Majh, given here in plain English, not word for word. It doesn't sound like a hymn. It sounds like a headline. No soft opening, no metaphor eased in gently, just three blunt pictures, one after another. And then, in the next breath, the lights go out. Today: the dark age is a knife, and what Guru Nanak sees in the dark.
screen: `THE AGE IS A KNIFE.` → `THE KINGS ARE BUTCHERS.` → `RIGHTEOUSNESS HAS FLOWN.`

segments.voice: The age in the line is Kal, the Kali Yuga, the dark age in the old Indian reckoning of time. Guru Nanak takes that name and makes it a blade. Here's how the salok goes on, again in plain English. Falsehood is the night of the new moon, and the moon of truth can't be seen rising anywhere. I've searched and searched, and I'm bewildered. In the darkness there's no path to be seen. People cry out in pain, caught in their own ego. Says Nanak, how will anyone be saved? Three things to notice. First, he names who holds the knife. Not demons, not fate. Kings, the people trusted with power, have become butchers. The Babarvani hymns, a few days back on this path, said something like it about an invasion. Here it widens into a picture of an age. Second, righteousness isn't killed. It flies. It grows wings and leaves, which means it was able to go, and might be able to return. Third, Nanak puts himself in the dark too. I've searched, I'm bewildered, I can't see the path. He doesn't stand above the age pointing down. He stands inside it, looking for the moon. And the salok ends on a question, not a slogan. How will anyone be saved? The ballad leaves that question standing, and other lines of the Var answer it with the Guru, the lamp it opened with. That's the shape of today's line. An age can cut. Power can butcher. Truth can hide like the moon on a dark night. And still someone keeps searching the sky for it. A knife of an age.
screen: `KAL: THE DARK AGE BECOMES A BLADE.` · `THE KINGS HAVE BECOME BUTCHERS.` · `TRUTH'S MOON CAN'T BE SEEN.` · `NANAK SEARCHES IN THE DARK.` · then, large: `A KNIFE OF AN AGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold honest rulers in mind. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind the people who hold power over your life: in your town, your country, your work. Don't argue with them in your head. Just see them, one at a time. Then picture the moon of truth rising over each of them, a small light in a dark sky. If you pray, you can ask God, in your own way, for honesty in those who lead. If you don't, you can simply wish it for them, and for the people under them. The bell holds the time.
The dark age is a knife. Guru Nanak's salok in Majh ki Var: the age cuts, kings are butchers, righteousness has flown, and truth's moon hides, while he keeps searching. Today's word.
screen: `THE DARK AGE IS A KNIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a knife of an age. Today, in one place where you hold a little power, at home, at work, online, use it honestly, the way you'd want a king to. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

what it means: Guru Nanak names an age where power cuts and truth hides, and stands inside it, still searching.
what a scholar hears: kal kati raje kasai, the age a knife and kings butchers; dharam grows wings and flies, an image of truth leaving, not dying.
